steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper announcing a competition on using ChatGPT prompts to generate levels for the game Science Birds that look like letters. Cover background on LLMs and their use in level generation, why we chose this platform and a competition format, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- ChatGPT and large language models, emergent abilities
- LLMs in robotics and procedural content generation
- Why Science Birds and letter-shaped levels
- Prompt engineering and the competition
- Goals, contributions, paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- ChatGPT and LLMs
  - 100 million users within two months; fastest application to reach it
  - powered by GPT-3.5 (OpenAI's Generative Pre-trained Transformer)
  - supervised fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback
  - GPT-3.5: 175B parameters; other LLMs 280B to 540B
  - Wei et al.: past a parameter threshold -> tasks without explicit training = emergent abilities
  - many use cases
- LLMs in robotics and PCG
  - Vemprala et al.: prompt structures for ChatGPT to output robot commands
  - PCG, esp. level generation
  - Todd et al.: fine-tuned GPT-2 variants, Sokoban levels, only starting token as input
  - Sudhakaran et al.: fine-tuned GPT-2, Mario levels from instructions
  - difference: capabilities exploration vs. controllable generation with text prompts
- Science Birds
  - clone of Angry Birds; stable levels with good weight distribution under gravity = hard
  - levels must resemble English capital letters -> careful, creative prompt design
- Prompt engineering and competition
  - prompt = text to communicate with an LM; PE = empirical process of designing prompts
  - empirical -> competition; best prompt for stable letter-like level
  - single prompt per participant; evaluated on all 26 capital letters
  - restrictions for simplicity; tools to speed up design
- Goals and contributions
  - push PE and PCG (level generation); understanding of ChatGPT emergent abilities
  - tools + modified Science Birds platform; sample prompt; experiments + ablation; spark interest
  - Sections II-V

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
ChatGPT is software that got 100 million users within two months of its release, which makes it the fastest application ever to reach that milestone. It runs on GPT-3.5, a fairly new version of a large language model (LLM) called Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) that was developed by OpenAI. ChatGPT is GPT-3.5 with supervised fine-tuning using reinforcement learning from human feedback so that it follows human instructions better. Recent LLMs like GPT-3.5 are very large, and GPT-3.5 alone has 175B parameters. Other LLMs with 280B to 540B parameters have also come out in recent years, and they have capabilities that smaller models do not have. Wei et al. found that when LLMs pass a certain threshold of parameter count they can do tasks without being explicitly trained for them, which are emergent abilities. Because of these emergent abilities ChatGPT has been used in various use cases.

One application of LLMs is robotics. In a report by Vemprala et al., the authors try different prompt structures to instruct ChatGPT, a conversational LLM, to output commands that control robots in various applications. Procedural content generation (PCG) is another area where LLMs could be useful, especially for level generation. There are already studies that apply LLMs to PCG. Todd et al. fine tuned variants of GPT-2 to generate levels for Sokoban, a puzzle game, with only the starting token as input to the model. A study by Sudhakaran et al. also used a fine-tuned version of GPT-2 to generate Mario levels from instructions. The main difference between these two studies is that the first one explored the capabilities of LLMs for level generation, while the second one focused on controllable level generation with text prompts.

These studies inspired us to look further into using ChatGPT for PCG. We chose Science Birds, a clone of Angry Birds, as the evaluation platform, because it is challenging to generate levels with good weight distribution that can withstand in-game gravity. To make it harder, the generated levels have to look like the shape of an English capital letter. To get such a level from ChatGPT, the prompt has to be designed carefully and creatively.

- Prompt engineering and competition
  - prompt = text to communicate with an LM; PE = empirical design of prompts
  - competition: best prompt for a stable level resembling an uppercase letter
  - one prompt per participant, evaluated on all 26 capital letters
  - restrictions for simplicity; tools to help
- Goals and contributions
  - push PE and PCG; understanding of ChatGPT and emergent abilities
  - tools + modified Science Birds; sample prompt; experiments + ablation; spark interest
  - outline: Sections II-V

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
ChatGPT is software that got 100 million users within two months of its release, which makes it the fastest application ever to reach that milestone. It runs on GPT-3.5, a fairly new version of a large language model (LLM) called Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) that was developed by OpenAI. ChatGPT is GPT-3.5 with supervised fine-tuning using reinforcement learning from human feedback so that it follows human instructions better. Recent LLMs like GPT-3.5 are very large, and GPT-3.5 alone has 175B parameters. Other LLMs with 280B to 540B parameters have also come out in recent years, and they have capabilities that smaller models do not have. Wei et al. found that when LLMs pass a certain threshold of parameter count they can do tasks without being explicitly trained for them, which are emergent abilities. Because of these emergent abilities ChatGPT has been used in various use cases.

One application of LLMs is robotics. In a report by Vemprala et al., the authors try different prompt structures to instruct ChatGPT, a conversational LLM, to output commands that control robots in various applications. Procedural content generation (PCG) is another area where LLMs could be useful, especially for level generation. There are already studies that apply LLMs to PCG. Todd et al. fine tuned variants of GPT-2 to generate levels for Sokoban, a puzzle game, with only the starting token as input to the model. A study by Sudhakaran et al. also used a fine-tuned version of GPT-2 to generate Mario levels from instructions. The main difference between these two studies is that the first one explored the capabilities of LLMs for level generation, while the second one focused on controllable level generation with text prompts.

These studies inspired us to look further into using ChatGPT for PCG. We chose Science Birds, a clone of Angry Birds, as the evaluation platform, because it is challenging to generate levels with good weight distribution that can withstand in-game gravity. To make it harder, the generated levels have to look like the shape of an English capital letter. To get such a level from ChatGPT, the prompt has to be designed carefully and creatively.

Here a prompt is a text used to communicate with a language model (LM) to get the response you want. Prompt engineering (PE) is the empirical process of designing a prompt to control how LMs behave. Since it is empirical, we decided to host a competition. The goal of the competition is to find the best prompt that can generate a stable level that looks like an English uppercase character. Participants can only submit one prompt. Each prompt is evaluated for all 26 English capital letters. We hope the competition encourages people to use creativity and skills to craft the prompt that gives the best results. For this we enforce some restrictions for simplicity and we provide various tools to help and speed up designing the prompt for the competition.

We hope the competition pushes the boundaries of PE and PCG, especially level generation. We expect the competition to give a better understanding of PE and PCG with LMs. We also hope it sparks interest in not just interacting with ChatGPT but also understanding it and its emergent abilities better. Our contributions are:

- 1. We provide tools and a platform, a modified version of Science Birds, to test ChatGPT responses for generating Science Birds levels.

- 2. We provide a sample prompt as a starting point that can be modified into better-performing prompts.

- 3. We run experiments and an ablation study on a modified version of our sample prompt to better understand how effective it is and some of its components.

- 4. We hope to spark interest in using ChatGPT for PCG.

Related work is in Section II, competition details are in Section III, the sample prompt, its modified version and variations and their performance are in Section IV, and conclusions are in Section V.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
ChatGPT [1] is software that reached 100 million users within two months of its release, making it the fastest application ever to reach that milestone [2]. It is powered by GPT-3.5, a relatively new version of a large language model (LLM) called Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) developed by OpenAI. ChatGPT is a supervised fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that uses reinforcement learning from human feedback to better follow human instructions [3]. Recent LLMs, including GPT-3.5, are remarkable in size, with GPT-3.5 alone having 175B parameters [3]. Other LLMs [4,5,6], with parameter counts ranging from 280B to 540B, have also been introduced in recent years, enabling capabilities not found in smaller models. Wei et al. [7] discovered that once LLMs reach a certain threshold of parameter count, they can perform tasks without explicit training, exhibiting emergent abilities. These emergent abilities have led to the use of ChatGPT in various use cases [8,9,10].

One notable application of LLMs is in robotics. In a report by Vemprala et al. [11], the authors explore different prompt structures to instruct ChatGPT, a conversational LLM, to output commands for controlling robots in various applications. Procedural content generation (PCG) is another area where LLMs could be useful, especially level generation. In fact, there are already studies on applying LLMs to PCG. Todd et al. [12] fine tuned variants of GPT-2 to generate levels for Sokoban, a puzzle game, using only the starting token as input to the model. Similarly, Sudhakaran et al. [13] applied a fine-tuned version of GPT-2 to generate Mario levels based on instructions. The key difference between these two studies is that the former explored the capabilities of LLMs for level generation, while the latter focused on controllable level generation using text prompts.

Inspired by these studies, we want to further investigate the application of ChatGPT to PCG. For this purpose, we have chosen Science Birds [14], a clone of Angry Birds, as our evaluation platform, because generating levels with good weight distribution that can withstand in-game gravity is challenging. To make it even more challenging, the generated levels must resemble the shape of an English capital letter. To obtain such a level through ChatGPT, one must design the prompt carefully and creatively.

A prompt, in this context, is a text used to communicate with a language model (LM) to get the desired response. Prompt engineering (PE) is the empirical process of designing a prompt to control the behavior of LMs [15]. Because of its empirical nature, we have decided to host a competition. The objective of this competition is to find the best prompt that can generate a stable level that looks like an English uppercase character. Participants may submit only a single prompt, and each prompt will be evaluated for all 26 English capital letters. We hope that this competition will encourage people to use both creativity and skill in crafting the prompt that yields the best results. To this end, we enforce some restrictions for simplicity and provide various tools to aid in and accelerate prompt design for the competition.

We hope that this competition will push the boundaries of PE and PCG, in particular level generation. Through the competition, we anticipate a better understanding of PE and PCG with LMs. We also hope to spark interest in not only interacting with ChatGPT but also gaining more understanding of it and its emergent abilities. Our contributions are as follows:

- 1. We provide tools and a platform, a modified version of Science Birds, for testing ChatGPT responses in generating levels for Science Birds.

- 2. We provide a sample prompt that serves as a starting point to modify for better-performing prompts.

- 3. We conduct experiments and an ablation study on a modified version of our sample prompt to better understand its effectiveness and some of its components.

- 4. We hope to spark interest in using ChatGPT for PCG.

We discuss related work in Section II, competition details in Section III, our sample prompt, its modified version and variations, and their performance in Section IV, and conclusions in Section V.
